Testimony of Ashley Luszczki Committee on Environment and Natural Resources
L.D. 2036, An Act to Clarify the Approval Process for and the Operation of the
Commingling Program for the Management of Beverage Containers
February 4, 2026
Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and members of the Committee on Environment and
Natural Resources, my name is Ashley Luszczki, and I am providing testimony on behalf of the
Maine State Chamber of Commerce, the state's largest business association. The Chamber supports innovation, economic competitiveness, and a predictable regulatory enviromnent that
allows businesses to thrive. With those principles in mind, we support L.D. 2036,
which establishes a clear, structured, and Department-approved framework for transitioning Maine to a more streamlined beverage container redemption program.
While the legislation is not prescriptive about day-to-day operations, it creates the conditions for
a thoughtful transition away from brand-based sorting toward material-based sorting. We believe
this transition is logical and timely. Sorting by material reflects how recycling markets function
today and mirrors the approach used in extended producer responsibility programs for
packaging. From an operational perspective, this model simplifies the sorting process for redemption centers by reducing the number of sorting streams and the amount of manual labor required to identify, separate, and track dozens of individual brands. Fewer sorting streams will result in more efficient processing, lower labor pressure, and reduced operating
costs.
Specific to L.D. 2036, and most importantly, is the clear and transparent structure
it establishes for how this transition will take place. The legislation places appropriate emphasis
on the development of a comprehensive plan that must be reviewed and approved by the Department. That plan is required to address key issues such as cost allocation, data reporting, auditing, timelines, and performance expectations, and it must include an element of public
input.
In particular, the use of sales data from initiators of deposit is central to making this system work fairly and effectively. Initiators already collect this information in the ordinaly course of business, and relying on verified sales data allows costs and responsibility to be allocated based on actual market activity, rather than estimates or brand-level counts generated at redemption
centers.
\7Vhile we support the operational shift to material-based sorting, the Chamber believes the true
value of L.D. 2036 lies in the clear regulatory expectations it sets for program design,

L.D. 2036: An Act to Clarify the Approval Process for and the Operation of the Commingling Program for the Management of Beverage Containers Testimony of: Brian Beneski, Supervisor, Recycling Programs Public Hearing: February 4, 2026 Page 2 of4
L.D. 2036 proposes two changes to the Beverage Container Redemption Program. It would allow the Commingling Cooperative to delay the commingling of beverage containers by material type, size and deposit value, rather than by commingling group and material type, size, and deposit value, until such time that initiators of deposit ("lODs") have provided auditable beverage container sales data to the Cooperative. Additionally, it removes the Department's processing and approval of the Cooperative's operations plan from the Department's requirements outlined in Department Rule, Chapter 2: Processing of Applications and other Administrative Matters. The Department is neither for nor against these changes, however the Department would like to point out several items for the committee to consider.
As written, L.D. 2036 will require a full transition from sorting by brand to material type
(full comingling) by October 1, 2026 only if 90% of lODs submit auditable sales data by
June 30, 2026. Requiring auditable sales data prior to full commingling will likely delay
implementation of this program for an uncertain amount of time, as it is unknown how many lODs collect what would be considered auditable sales data. Unless there is a
specific definition and an incentive or a target date requiring lODs to start collecting this
data, it is possible that this requirement may never be achieved. Since there is no definition of "auditable beverage container sales data," or any indication as to who is
responsible for this definition, this goal is open to interpretation and will lead to uncertainty within the regulated community. Finally, it should also be noted that the share of beverages on the beverage market belonging to individual lODs varies considerably; a few lODs contribute a large percentage to the market, whereas a large number of smaller lODs each contribute only a small percentage of containers. Therefore, the number of lODs reporting auditable sales data is not reflective of the extent to which beverages sold are being accounted for within the beverage container redemption system.

lf this bill moves fon/vard, the Department recommends the following: - Providing language to incentivize or require a target date upon which individual lODs must begin to collect and report "auditable" sales data. - Providing language to clarify that full comingling must occur within a given
timeframe once the 90% reporting goal has been reached.
- Providing a definition of auditable beverage container sales data.
Maine's Beverage Container law at 38 M.R.S. 3107 (3-B)(C)(1) establishes procedures for the Department's review of the Commingling Cooperative's operations plan, including steps for final approval of the plan if the Department requires the Cooperative
to make revisions to the plan. This paragraph authorizes the Department to approve a revised plan "subject to the implementation of specific changes required by the department." In other words, if the Department determines that the plan does not meet the requirements of the statute, the Department may impose specific changes in the
Cooperative's plan and then issue a final approval.
L.D. 2036 specifies that approval of the plan submitted by the Cooperative would not be considered to be a "license or permit decision or other final action of the Department" in accordance with provisions outlined in Department's Chapter 2` . lt is important to consider that Chapter 2 was developed to ensure that there is a specific, defined process for the Department to review applications and issue Department decisions in order to provide consistency. By following these rules, the Department provides clarity to the regulated community as well as transparency. As part of this process, Chapter 2 also provides a pathway for any applicant that wishes to appeal a final agency action. If the approval of the plan is no longer subject to the rules regarding the processing of applications, the Commingling Cooperative would no longer have a venue to challenge
the Department's decision on the Cooperative's operations plan. lt is unclear why

Dan Tarr Belfast LD 2036
Thank you for the opportunity to submit written testimony regarding changes to Maine's Bottle Bill. My name is Dan Tarr, and I am the owner of Easterly Wine, a small wine distribution business in Belfast, Maine. I specialize in distributing high-quality, small production wines, many of which are produced by family-owned wineries in Europe and other regions. I respectfully submit this testimony in opposition to the portion of the Bottle Bill that requires UPCs on wine labels. While I understand and appreciate the intent of standardizing product identification and improving regulatory oversight, a mandatory UPC requirement would have significant unintended consequences for small distributors. Many high-end and artisanal wines do not carry UPCs and, in many cases, cannot reasonably add them. These producers often bottle in very small quantities, use traditional labeling methods, or export to multiple markets with different regulatory requirements. Requiring UPCs would in many cases make it impossible for these wines to be sold in our state at all. As a small distributor, I do not have the leverage to require foreign or small producers to redesign labels or alter their bottling processes solely for one market. The result would be a loss of unique products, reduced consumer choice, and a competitive disadvantage for small businesses like mine. Maine's wine market is recognized in the industry as being far more sophisticated than its population size would indicate. This bill would also affect restaurants, retailers, and consumers who value access to distinctive, high-quality wines that are rare, special, and highly sought-after. Ultimately, the economic impact would fall disproportionately on small businesses while offering limited additional benefit in terms of compliance or enforcement. I respectfully urge the Committee to consider aspects to the bill, such as exemptions for limited-production wines, alternative identification methods, or thresholds that recognize the realities of small-scale wine production and distribution. Thank you for your time and consideration. I appreciate the Committee's work and your willingness to hear from small business owners who will be directly affected by this legislation. Respectfully submitted, Dan Tarr Easterly Wine Belfast

Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and distinguished members ofthe Environment and Natural
Resources Committee, my name is Vanessa Berry, and l am the Sustainable Maine Program Manager
for the Natural Resources Council of Maine (N RCM). l appreciate this opportunity to testify in opposition to LD 2036.
in 2023, this Committee took important steps to modernize Maine's Bottle Bill at a time when many local redemption centers were facing serious financial strain, with some shutting their doors permanently. To keep redemption centers in business, the 131*` Legislature increased handling fees (LD 134) and made several improvements to reduce the number of container sorts and lower operational
costs (LD 1909). While redemption centers were extremely encouraged by these overdue changes, the
full benefits from LD 1909 will not be realized until the law is fully implemented.
Before addressing our specific concerns with the amended bill that we received only yesterday, l should note
that we have not had suflicient time to fully review and analyze the Sponsor's amendment. We have identified
several initial concerns worth flagging for the Committee that would cause delays or weaken Maine's Bottle
Bill, and we may have additional concerns that we will provide in advance of the work session on LD 2036.
New Barriers to Commingling and Efficiency First, the amendment would require that 9o percent of initiators of Deposit (iODs) provide
"auditable beverage container sales data" before transitioning to full commingling ofcontainers. Without any enforcement and compliance mechanism in place, this provision would create a pathway for delays and force redemption centers to continue sorting by brand, undermining the efficiencies the Legislature intended through LD 1909.
Reduced Oversight and Performance Accountability The amendment would replace third-party audits with less rigorous "reviews" offinancial reporting and performance measures like redemption rates. it also would remove evaluation of regional redemption rates. This would limit the state's ability to assess whether convenience standards are working and to identify gaps in recycling access or education.
Reduced Financial Transparency and Fairness The amendment would reduce transparency around cooperative startup costs and how fair payments to cornmingling groups would be determined. These are core financial components of the program, and reducing visibility into these processes could create a situation where some pay beyond their fair share.

Removal of Clear implementation Deadlines
